scenario.title: Ares Deep
scenario.setting: Ares Deep is a five-person research outpost dug into the rim of Hellas Planitia on Mars, 214 sols into a 500-sol rotation. The nearest help is a cargo lander nine weeks out, and Earth is 14 light-minutes away. The station is cramped; everyone knows everyone's habits, but not their secrets. Whether the program gets a second rotation depends on what this crew sends home.
rules: Grounded near-future technology. No aliens, no magic. Any biological discovery is microbial at most and must stay scientifically plausible.
Mars is lethal: suit breaches, CO2 buildup, cold, radiation and dust are real dangers. Going outside requires a suit.
Messages to Earth take 14 minutes each way. There is no real-time help.
The crew are capable professionals under strain. Conflict comes from personality, pressure and secrets, not villainy.

scenario.opening:
The coffee substitute tastes like hot cardboard, same as every morning. What isn't the same is the sound: the water recycler in hydroponics has picked up a dry, unhealthy rattle that carries all the way into the commons.

Okafor sits at the galley table with her tablet, reading the overnight weather relay. "Dust storm building east of us," she says without looking up. "Twenty hours, maybe less. I want the arrays secured and the Mule inside by tonight."

Teo hovers by the galley counter, eyes on the recycler readout, unusually quiet. Somewhere down the corridor the lab door has been sealed since before you woke; that's Lev. Then the intercom crackles: Priya, from the garage, asking whether anyone has signed off on the Mule's battery swap yet, because she is not doing it twice.

It's going to be a long sol.

characterData.name: Dr. Lev Sorensen
characterData.want: be the first person to confirm life on Mars
characterData.secret: Cultures from the deep ice core are showing activity he cannot explain as contamination. He has told no one and keeps the samples in an unlogged incubator.

characterData.name: Priya Raman

recent.text:
"Here — I'll help with that," you say, already up. "Takes half the time with two of us. Then I get to the arrays faster."

Teo's face does something complicated. "Sure — yeah, great." He's backing toward the corridor, hands still moving. "It's just the housing, two clips and it's out, I'll grab the spare. You don't have to look at the log or anything, it's boring, honestly."

Okafor pockets her tablet. "Keep it under an hour, both of you. I want a number, not a shrug." She's gone toward Ops before you can answer.

In Hydroponics the grow racks hum purple and the recycler knocks away at seventy percent. Teo talks the whole time — filter tolerances, the spare he's sure is on the shelf, a story about his cousin's aquarium — and plants himself between you and the panel, both hands on the filter housing like it might bolt. The clips come off clean. The filter underneath is grey, but it isn't six days grey.

The intercom crackles. Sorensen, from the lab, soft and quick: "Ah — Kit, Imani — small thing. Whatever the storm does to the power budget, my incubator keeps priority. It's — it's delicate work. Nothing to worry about." A pause. "Please." The channel clicks dead before anyone can ask what's in it.

log.text:
You set your mug down and ask Okafor straight: what do you want me on first. She doesn't look up from the tablet. "The recycler. If it drops below fifty percent we're rationing by tomorrow, and I won't have that conversation with Mission Control." Now she does look at you, level. "Arrays after. I want you suited and back inside before the dust hits. Teo can help with the water side."

"It's — honestly it's probably just the filter," Teo says, too fast, stepping away from the counter. "I've been meaning to change it, I can do it myself, you don't need to tear the whole thing down, that's a lot of hours for a filter —" He's already moving toward the corridor, wiping his hands on his trousers like he's been caught at something.

For most of the hour you're at the galley table with the recycler's schematics up on your tablet, cross-referencing the fault codes against the last six nights of Teo's shift logs, while Okafor works through her storm checklist across from you. Then the intercom crackles from the garage, flatter than before. "Anyone signing off on the Mule's battery swap, or should I just guess?"

You set your mug down and ask Okafor straight: what do you want me on first. She doesn't look up from the tablet. "The recycler. If it drops below fifty percent we're rationing by tomorrow, and I won't have that conversation with Mission Control." Now she does look at you, level. "Arrays after. I want you suited and back inside before the dust hits. Teo can help with the water side."

"It's — honestly it's probably just the filter," Teo says, too fast, stepping away from the counter. "I've been meaning to change it, I can do it myself, you don't need to tear the whole thing down, that's a lot of hours for a filter —" He's already moving toward the corridor, wiping his hands on his trousers like he's been caught at something.
